source_read: PMC HTML full text, PMC3043109 (BMJ 2011;342:d671), read in full in the built-in browser: abstract, introduction, methods, results, Table 1 (study list, country column tallied) and Table 2, discussion, limitations, implications, boxes, contributors, funding and competing interests. Figures 1-7 (flow chart and forest plots) not examined as images; their pooled values are in Table 2 and the text. Web appendix (tables of adjustment per study, cumulative meta-analyses) not read.

claims.note: Every Ronksley 2011 number in the statement and magnitude matches Table 2 and the text: any drinking 0.71 (0.66-0.77; 29 studies), 0.75 (0.68-0.81; 31) and 0.75 (0.70-0.80; 21). By intake: 0.96, 0.75, 0.66, 0.67, 0.76 (0.52-1.09) and 0.92, 0.79, 0.79, 0.77, 0.75 (0.63-0.89). Lifetime abstainers 0.73 (9 studies), 0.75 (7), 0.82 (9). Former drinkers 1.31, 1.48, 1.10. I2 72.2%. 12.5 g per drink when not stated. 8 of 84 studies unadjusted only. The table-versus-text discrepancy on the former-drinker comparison is correctly described. 'Mostly high-income countries' holds: about 8 of 87 Table 1 rows are from China (6), Serbia and Montenegro, and Russia. 'Most studies' non-drinkers included former drinkers' is an inference the paper does not count. It is consistent with the paper, since only 4 to 8 studies per outcome separated former drinkers and 3 to 9 used lifetime abstainers. Small qualifications: (1) another 8 studies adjusted only for basic demographics, so 16 of 84 had at most demographic adjustment; (2) the '0.66 to 0.79' range at higher intakes includes one estimate whose interval crosses 1 (incident CHD above 60 g, 0.76, 0.52-1.09); (3) at under 2.5 g a day, cardiovascular mortality was 0.71 (0.57-0.89; 7 studies) and new stroke 0.81 (0.74-0.89; 3). Such large associations at under half a drink a day are hard to attribute to alcohol and fit the claim's doubts about the comparison group. The authors argue for causation (Hill's criteria, companion biomarker review) and say including former drinkers 'did not seem to bias' the association. The claim correctly treats causation as disputed and does not adopt that argument. Arithmetic: 12.5 g per drink; 14.9 g a day is about 1.2 drinks of 12.5 g. 'Up to about one drink' follows the paper's own '(about ≤1 drink)'.

anchors.locator: Methods › Study selection, 2nd paragraph; Methods › Data extraction and quality assessment, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Prospective cohorts of adults 18 or over without pre-existing cardiovascular disease. Exposure: current drinking at baseline against non-drinkers. Lifetime-abstainer reference groups, and studies separating former drinkers, were identified as subsets. Intake in g a day, with 12.5 g per drink where a study gave no grams. Categories under 2.5 g (under half a drink), 2.5-14.9 (about half to one drink), 15-29.9, 30-60, over 60 g a day.

anchors.locator: Results › Identification of studies, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (Country column); Abstract › Data sources
anchors.extracted: Medline and Embase to September 2009, any language. 4235 citations, 84 studies: 34 all-male cohorts, 6 women only, 44 both. Table 1 country column (87 rows): USA 35, Japan 7, China 6, Australia 6, Finland 6, Denmark 5, UK 4, Canada 3, others 1-2 each (including Serbia and Montenegro, Russia, Puerto Rico, Poland, a multinational European cohort).
Follow-up 2.5 to 35 years (mean 11). Confounders adjusted for ranged from none to 18 (mean 6). 68 studies gave adjusted estimates; 8 gave only unadjusted and 8 adjusted only for basic demographics.

anchors.extracted: At under 2.5 g a day: CVD mortality 0.71 (0.57-0.89; 7 studies), incident stroke 0.81 (0.74-0.89; 3). These are as low as or lower than at higher intakes, at under half a drink a day.

anchors.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph; Discussion › An argument for causation, 1st-2nd paragraphs; Discussion › Implications, 1st paragraph; What this study adds
anchors.extracted: The authors say inclusion of former drinkers did not seem to bias the association. They build a causal case from Hill's criteria and their companion biomarker review, and suggest counselling selected patients to drink moderately (to be tested in trials). These are interpretations; the data are observational relative risks with no absolute risks.

claims.note: Every Ronksley 2011 number in the statement and magnitude matches. Incident stroke 0.98 (0.91-1.06; 17 studies); stroke death 1.06 (0.91-1.23; 10). Against lifetime abstainers 0.93 (0.85-1.02; 7) and 1.29 (1.09-1.53; 3). Incident stroke by intake 0.81 (3 studies), 0.80 (3), 0.92, 1.15, 1.62 (1.32-1.98; 4). Haemorrhagic 1.14 (0.97-1.34; 12); ischaemic 0.92 (0.85-1.00; 8). Ronksley gives relative risks only, no absolute risks. Qualifications the claim omits: stroke death was lower at 2.5-14.9 g a day (0.86, 0.75-0.99; 6 studies), and the abstract puts the lowest stroke-mortality risk at one drink a day or less. Stroke death was higher in weakly adjusted studies (1.30, 1.11-1.52; 5) and with long follow-up (1.18, 1.02-1.37; 5). Women showed lower stroke risk (0.87, 0.75-1.01; and 0.81, 0.67-0.98, from 4 and 3 studies). Only two studies gave stroke results for former drinkers against non-drinkers. 'Most groups including former drinkers' is an inference, as for the heart claim. None of these change the claim's summary for cohort studies.

key_findings.correction: Confirmed. The 'did not seem to bias' sentence is in Discussion, 4th paragraph (counted).
Confirmed: Methods › Data synthesis and analysis, 3rd running-text paragraph if the displayed formulas are not counted; Results › Sensitivity analyses, 2nd and 4th paragraphs.
Confirmed: ref 106 is the US Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2005.

reporting_issues.note: Confirmed: Burke 2007 is listed with ages 15-88 (Table 1); ref 53 (Hammar 1997) is titled a case referent study based on the Swedish Twin Register. Both contribute to incident CHD.

Confirmed as printed: Garg (Table 1 1992, ref 47 1993) and Rehm 1997 are both NHANES. Solomon 2000 (ref 90, women with type 2 diabetes) is listed with 121,700 NHS participants. Chiuve 2008 has 71,243 and Fuchs 1995 85,709. The parent-cohort reading is an inference.
Confirmed: 'Brusselton' in Table 1 against 'Busselton' in ref 33; Garg 1992 against 1993; the women's stroke strata have 4 and 3 studies.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2, critically low. Items 2 and 7 fail clearly: the protocol is unregistered and undescribed, and there is no list of excluded studies. Items 9, 11 and 13 'no' are defensible: covariate counts are used instead of a risk-of-bias tool; unadjusted estimates are pooled without justification and within-study categories are pooled as if independent; the causal argument is made despite these limits. Item 9 could be read as partial yes; the overall rating would not change. Sample details checked: study sizes range from 286 to 581,321; the Physicians' Health Study appears 4 times and the Nurses' Health Study, Framingham, Kaiser Permanente and Copenhagen City Heart Study 3 times each; Mukamal is an author of refs 77, 78, 79 and 94.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. All six listed gaps were checked against the text: the 'confirm the beneficial effects' box; the dose-response criterion contradicted by Table 2; 'adjusted' in the abstract; the abstract's lowest risk at 1-2 drinks; the reference-group sensitivity analysis described as no change; and 'compared with abstaining'. The counselling and public-health proposals in Implications push it towards severe.

missed: Interpretive point not on the card: at under 2.5 g a day (under 0.2 of a 12.5-g drink), CVD mortality was 0.71 (0.57-0.89; 7 studies) and incident stroke 0.81 (0.74-0.89; 3) (Table 2). These associations are as strong as or stronger than at higher intakes and are hard to attribute to alcohol. They point to differences between the reference group and very light drinkers, which the authors do not discuss.

Three included cohorts were selected for diabetes: Diem 2003 (ref 35, type 2 diabetes), Valmadrid 1999 (ref 97, older-onset diabetes) and Solomon 2000 (ref 90, women with type 2 diabetes). They are not excluded by the stated criterion, which names only cardiovascular disease, but they are illness-selected samples. This should be added to the card's selection effects.
